title: Minneapolis: City of Lakes Where Prince Was King
summary: Minnesota's largest city where 13 lakes lie within city limits, where Prince created his Minneapolis Sound, where flour mills made it 'Mill City,' and where 11 miles of skyways let you walk all winter without ever going outside.

content.intro: Minneapolis should not exist. The climate is brutal - January averages 16°F, the Mississippi freezes solid, and winter seems to last forever. Yet 400,000 people live here, and they seem to like it. They bicycle in bike lanes even in November, swim in one of the 13 lakes within city limits, and walk through 11 miles of enclosed skyways connecting 80 blocks of downtown so completely that some residents go entire winters without wearing a coat outside. The city grew from St. Anthony Falls, the only major waterfall on the Mississippi, whose power ran lumber mills then flour mills that made Minneapolis 'Mill City,' producing more flour than any city on Earth by 1880. Pillsbury and General Mills still have headquarters here. But Minneapolis today means something else: it means Prince, who was born here in 1958, created the Minneapolis Sound at First Avenue and Paisley Park, and made this frozen city the center of popular music for a decade. The purple rain still falls.

sections.title: Chain of Lakes
sections.body: Thirteen lakes lie entirely within Minneapolis city limits - more than any other American city. The Chain of Lakes (Cedar, Lake of the Isles, Calhoun/Bde Maka Ska, Harriet) connects by parkways designed by landscape architect Horace Cleveland in the 1880s, creating a system of lakes, paths, and green spaces that circles the southwestern quadrant of the city. On summer weekends, the lakes teem with sailors, kayakers, paddleboarders, swimmers at public beaches. The paths fill with runners, cyclists, rollerbladers circling the water. Winter transforms the lakes into skating rinks and ice fishing spots. Lake Harriet's band shell hosts free concerts; Lake Calhoun (officially renamed Bde Maka Ska in 2018 to honor the Dakota name) anchors the chain. Minneapolis exists because of water power; it thrives because of these waters.

sections.title: Mill City
sections.body: St. Anthony Falls powered Minneapolis's growth - first sawmills processing Minnesota's vast northern forests, then flour mills grinding wheat from the prairie. By 1880, Minneapolis produced more flour than any city in the world; Pillsbury A Mill was the world's largest. The mills declined as wheat production shifted to the northern plains, but the ruins remain. Mill City Museum occupies the remnants of the Washburn A Mill, dramatically destroyed by a flour dust explosion in 1878 (flour dust is explosive - 18 workers died). The Stone Arch Bridge, built in 1883 to carry trains across the falls, now carries pedestrians and cyclists. The Mill District has become apartments and restaurants; the Guthrie Theater's cantilevered lobby frames views of the river. What powered the city's rise is now its most distinctive neighborhood.

sections.title: Prince's Minneapolis
sections.body: Prince Rogers Nelson was born in Minneapolis in 1958, and he never really left. First Avenue, the downtown nightclub, became world famous when 'Purple Rain' was filmed there in 1983. Prince built Paisley Park in suburban Chanhassen - his home, recording studio, and creative headquarters, now a museum where the purple piano sits and the vault of unreleased recordings remains. The Minneapolis Sound - synth-driven funk with rock guitar and R&B vocals - influenced everything that came after, from Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis producing Janet Jackson to the broader pop landscape of the 1980s. Prince died at Paisley Park in 2016; the city mourned in purple. First Avenue still hosts shows; the purple lights still shine on Hennepin Avenue. Minneapolis was never just Prince's backdrop - it shaped his sound, and he shaped how the world heard Minneapolis.

sections.title: Skyway City
sections.body: Minneapolis's skyway system connects 80 blocks of downtown through 11 miles of enclosed, climate-controlled bridges. You can walk from the North Loop to the convention center without ever stepping outside - useful when it's 10 below and the wind is blowing. The skyways created a second level of retail and food courts, a parallel city above the streets. Critics argue they drained street-level vitality; defenders note they make winter livable. Either way, the system is unique in its extent. Downtown Minneapolis also hosts the largest Somali population in North America, refugees from civil war who arrived in the 1990s and built a community centered on Cedar-Riverside. The city's demographics have transformed - more than 17% of Minnesotans now speak a language other than English at home, many of them Somali, Hmong, or Spanish.

sections.title: Twin Cities Position
sections.body: Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport (MSP) is a major Delta hub with extensive domestic and international connections. The Twin Cities are literally twin - Minneapolis and St. Paul share a metro area but maintain distinct identities, Minneapolis the larger and younger, St. Paul the state capital and more traditionally Midwestern. I-94 connects them; I-35 splits into I-35W (Minneapolis) and I-35E (St. Paul). The Metro Transit light rail connects the airport to both downtowns. From altitude, Minneapolis appears as development around lakes - the Chain of Lakes visible in the southwest, the Mississippi curving through downtown, the Stone Arch Bridge crossing at St. Anthony Falls. What appears from the air as a frozen Midwestern city is where flour made fortunes, where Prince made music, and where lakes make winter survivable.

content.flightContext: Located at 44.98°N, 93.27°W on the Mississippi River in southeastern Minnesota. From altitude, Minneapolis appears as a city defined by water - 13 lakes within city limits, the Chain of Lakes circling the southwest, the Mississippi curving through downtown past the ruins of flour mills at St. Anthony Falls. What appears from the air as Minnesota's largest city is Mill City, where flour mills once ground more wheat than anywhere on Earth, and Prince's city, where the Minneapolis Sound was created.
